t.1.220.1: Janamejaya said: For what reason did Agni not burn the Śārṅgakas when that forest, having come to such a state, was being burnt? O Brahmin, tell me this quickly.
t.1.220.2: The reason for the non-burning of Aśvasena and of the Dānava Maya has indeed been told, O Brahman, but that of the Śārṅgakas has not been told.
t.1.220.3: O Brahmin, that non-destruction of the Śārṅgas is a marvel; tell me, in that onslaught of fire, how were they not destroyed?
t.1.220.4: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Why Agni did not burn the Śārṅgakas when things had come to such a pass, all that I shall tell you just as it happened, O Bhārata.
t.1.220.5: There was a great seer, learned in the scriptures, foremost among those who know the dharma, an ascetic of strict vows, renowned by the name Mandapāla.
t.1.220.6: He, O king, had taken up the path of the seers who are chaste and hold their seed upward; devoted to the study of the Veda, delighting in dharma, an ascetic, he had conquered his senses.
t.1.220.7: Having gone to the far shore of austerity and cast off his body, O Bhārata, he went to the world of the ancestors, but there he did not obtain that fruit.
t.1.220.8: Seeing that the worlds he had won even through austerity were fruitless, he questioned the celestials who stood near Dharmarāja.
t.1.220.9: Why are these worlds of mine, which I won through austerity, closed to me? What did I leave undone there, that this should be the fruit of that deed?
t.1.220.11: Men are born as debtors, O brahmin; hear that by which their debts are discharged: by sacred rites, by the life of celibate study, and by offspring. Of this there is no doubt.
t.1.220.12: All that debt is discharged through sacrifice, austerity, and sons. You are an ascetic and a performer of sacrifices, but you have no offspring.
t.1.220.10: There I shall do that for the sake of which this has been barred; tell me, O dwellers of heaven, what the fruit of this austerity is.
t.1.220.13: These worlds of yours are closed off on account of offspring. Beget offspring, and then you shall enjoy the eternal worlds.
t.1.220.14: A son rescues his father from the hell called Put, O sage; therefore, O best of the twice-born, strive for the continuation of your line through offspring.
t.1.220.15: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of the heaven-dwellers, Mandapāla pondered, "Where indeed might offspring come to me quickly and in abundance?"
t.1.220.16: Reflecting thus, he went to the birds that are abundant in offspring, and, having become a śārṅgaka bird, he approached Jaritā, a female śārṅgikā.
t.1.220.17: On her he begot four sons who were expounders of the Veda. Abandoning them right there, his young sons still in their eggs, together with their mother in the forest, the sage went off to Lapitā.
t.1.220.19: Abandoned by him in the forest, those sages who should never have been abandoned, her little sons still within their eggs, the distressed Jaritā did not forsake in Khāṇḍava, O king; and when they were born, overwhelmed by affection, she nourished them by her own means of livelihood.
t.1.220.18: When that illustrious one had gone off to Lapitā, O Bhārata, Jaritā, distressed by her love for her offspring, brooded deeply.
t.1.220.20: Then the seer Mandapāla, wandering in that forest together with Lapitā, saw Agni approaching to burn the Khāṇḍava.
t.1.220.23: The seers call you one, and again they call you threefold; having fashioned you eightfold, they made you the bearer of the sacrifice.
t.1.220.21: Understanding his resolve, and knowing that his sons were still small children, the brahmin seer, afraid, praised Jātavedas, the mighty guardian of the world, entrusting his sons to him.
t.1.220.22: You, O Agni, are the mouth of all the gods; you are the bearer of oblations. You, O Pāvaka, move hidden as the inner core of all beings.
t.1.220.24: The supreme seers say that this whole universe was created by you, O Hutāśana; for without you the entire world would instantly cease to be.
t.1.220.25: Having paid homage to you, the brahmins, together with their wives and their sons as well, go to the eternal goal won by their own deeds.
t.1.220.28: By you the waters were created in the beginning; in you rests this entire world. In you the offerings to the gods and the offerings to the ancestors are duly established.
t.1.220.27: O Jātavedas of great splendor, this creation of the universe is yours alone; yours alone is the ordained work, and all that exists, the moving and the unmoving.
t.1.220.26: O Agni, they call you the clouds that hang in the sky together with their lightning. The years, going forth from you, burn all beings.
t.1.220.30: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus praised by that Mandapāla, O king, Pāvaka was then pleased with that sage of boundless splendor, and with a gladdened heart he said to him, "What that you desire shall I do for you?"
t.1.220.29: O Agni, you alone are the blazing fire; you are Dhātṛ, you are Bṛhaspati. You are the twin Aśvins, you are Mitra and Soma, and you are Anila, the wind.
t.1.220.32: Promising that with the words "So be it," the blessed Havyavāhana, at that time, blazed up in the Khāṇḍava with the desire to burn it.
t.1.220.31: Mandapāla, with joined palms, said to him, the bearer of oblations: "As you burn the Khāṇḍava forest, spare my sons."
